**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 109, verses 1–3:**

﴿Say: O you disbelievers!﴾ ﴿I do not worship what you worship,﴾ ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship.﴾

Its opening with (قُلْ) "Say" serves to draw attention to what follows the command to speak, namely that it is a statement meant to be conveyed to people in a specific manner, stated explicitly, in that he is sent with a word to deliver. Otherwise, the entire Qur'an is commanded to be conveyed. There are parallels to this verse in the Qur'an that open with a command to speak, not in answer to a question from them: ﴿Say: O you who are Jews, if you claim that you are allies of God﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 6] in Surat al-Jumu'ah. The surahs that open with a command to speak are five: "Qul Uhiya" (Surat al-Jinn), Surat al-Kafirun, Surat al-Ikhlas, and the two Mu'awwidhatayn. The first three are for a word he conveys, and the two Mu'awwidhatayn are for a word he says to seek refuge for himself.

The address is directed to the four men who said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Let us worship what you worship, and you worship what we worship," as is in the report about the occasion of revelation. This is what the statement "nor are you worshippers of what I worship," as will come, requires.

Their address was begun with the call (nida') in order to convey it to them, because the call demands that their minds turn attentively to what will be said to them.

They were addressed by the description of disbelievers, to belittle them and to confirm the aspect of disassociation from them, and as a notification that he does not fear them when he addresses them with what they dislike, what arouses their anger, because God has sufficed him against them and protected him from their harm. Al-Qurtubi said: Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is: Say to those who disbelieve, "O you disbelievers!" so that he confronts them in their assembly and says to them, "O you disbelievers!" while they become angry at being attributed to disbelief.

So his statement, ﴿I do not worship what you worship,﴾ is an informing about himself of what has occurred from him.

The meaning is: my worship will not occur, of what you worship, at any times in the future, with certainty; because the imperfect verb (al-mudari') admits of both the present and the future, so when the negating (لا) enters upon it, it conveys its negation in future times, as was adopted in al-Kashshaf, and this is the view of the majority of the scholars of Arabic grammar. For this reason the particle (لَنْ) conveys emphasis of negation in the future beyond the basic negation. Accordingly, al-Khalil said: the origin of (لَنْ) is (لا أنْ). Since (لا) alone conveyed negation of the future, the assumption of (أنْ) after (لا) conveyed emphasis of that negation in the future. Therefore they said that (لَنْ) conveys emphasis of negation in the future, and so we know that (لا) conveyed negation of the action in the future. Ibn Malik disagreed with them, as in Mughni al-Labib, and so did Abu Hayyan, as he said in this surah, and al-Suhayli in his discussion of the revelation of this surah in al-Rawd al-Unuf.

The negation of his worship of their gods in the future conveys the negation of his worshipping them in the present, by the indication of the implication of the address (fahwa al-khitab), and because they only proposed to him that he worship their gods after a future year.

For this reason, in the matter of negating their worship of God, the negation came with the active participle (ism al-fa'il), which is truly in the present, in his saying: ﴿nor are you worshippers﴾, meaning: you are not, now, changing your polytheism, because they proposed to him that they would begin themselves and worship the Lord whom the Prophet ﷺ worships for a year. By this you will know the aspect of contrast between the structure of the two sentences in the eloquent usage of the language.

This is his informing them that he knows they will not do that from now on, through God Most High informing His Prophet ﷺ of that. So his statement here is one of the signs of his prophethood, like the saying of God Most High: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24], for none of those four men became Muslim, and they died in their polytheism.

What is meant by ﴿what I worship﴾ is God Most High, and he expressed it with the relative pronoun (ما), because it is established for the rational and for other than the rational of what is chosen, whereas (مَن) is specific to the rational. There is no obstacle to using (ما) for the rational when confusion is secure. Al-Suhayli said in al-Rawd al-Unuf: the relative (ما) is used with the intention of vagueness, to convey exaggeration in magnification, like the Arabs' saying: "Glory be to what the thunder glorifies with its praise," and the saying of God Most High: ﴿And the heaven and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5], as has already been mentioned in Surat al-Shams.

This serves to despair them of what they had sought from him, and to match their rejected statement with a similar one in conveying permanence.

The past tense verb appears in His words ﴿what you have worshipped﴾ (ما عَبَدْتُمْ) to indicate the firm entrenchment of them in the worship of idols over times that have passed. In it there is an allusion to the Prophet's (ﷺ) freedom from the worship of idols throughout past times. Otherwise, it would have said: "nor am I a worshipper of what we used to worship."

[p. 583]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 109, verse 5:

﴿And neither are you worshippers of what I worship.﴾

It is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 4], to explain the complete difference between their state and his state, and it is a second statement that they do not worship God. This second statement serves as an alert that God informed him that they do not worship God, and it strengthens the indication of these two statements as a prophetic report (nubuwwa). For he reported about them that, and all of those people died in disbelief, and this surah was among the proofs of prophethood.

From the mention of this clause alongside its like preceding it, there arises an emphasis (tawkid) of the preceding clause, emphasizing the original meaning of it. Its position is not the position of emphasis because of the presence of the conjunctive waw (wa al-ʿatf), as you have known a moment ago in his saying: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 4].

Therefore, the waw in his saying here, ﴿wa la antum ʿabidun ma aʿbud﴾, conjoins a clause to a clause, because of the relevance (munasaba) that the clause ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 4] required.

It is permissible that the clause ﴿And neither are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ be a verbal emphasis (tawkid lafzi) of its like preceding it in its entirety, with the waw of conjunction that is in its preceding like, and that the clause ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 4] be interposed between the emphasis and what is emphasized.

The purpose of the emphasis is to establish the refutation of their claim that they worship the Lord of Muhammad (ﷺ).

[p. 585 begins here]

*Tadhyil* (a concluding statement that reinforces the meaning) and *fadhlaka* (a summarizing conclusion) of the preceding discourse, with the emphases it contains. This statement was used as a proverb (*mathal*), and it is more comprehensive and concise than the verse of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, though our opinions differ.*

In the Tafsir of al-Fakhr (al-Razi) here, it occurs: "It has become the custom of people to recite this verse as a farewell formula, and that is not permissible, for He, the Exalted, did not send down the Qur'an to be recited as a proverb, but to be contemplated and then acted upon." End of quotation.

This statement is not carefully considered, for reciting it as a proverb does not contradict acting upon its meaning. Reciting it is in fact part of the completeness of its eloquence and a preparation for acting upon it. Al-Fakhr omitted this portion of the commentary from his draft.

In both clauses, the predicate is placed before the subject (*al-musnad ʿalayhi*) in order to express restriction (*qasr*) of the subject to the predicate. That is: "Your religion is restricted to being yours; it does not extend to being mine." And "My religion is restricted to being mine; it does not extend to being yours." That is, they are certain not to become Muslims. Thus the restriction is *qasr al-ifrad* (restriction that rejects a particular partnership), and the *lam* in both places denotes a semblance of ownership, which is exclusivity (*ikhtisas*) or entitlement (*istihqaq*).

*Din* (religion) means creed and community. It consists of knowledge and beliefs that a person holds, such that his actions follow their requirements. For this reason it is called *din*, since the original meaning of *din* is dealing and recompense.

Most readers recite *(dini)* without a *ya* after the *nun*, on the basis that the *ya* of the first person is elided for lightness, with the *kasra* retained on the *nun*. Yaʿqub recites it with the *ya* included both in continuous recitation (*wasl*) and at pause (*waqf*). This word is written in the Mushaf without a *ya*, relying on the memorization of the memorizers. The one who pronounces the *ya*, like Yaʿqub, extends the *kasra*, since the *ya* is merely the lengthening of the *kasra*. Its absence in the script therefore does not require its omission in pronunciation.

[p. 585 continues]

Nafiʿ, al-Bazzi on the authority of Ibn Kathir, Hisham on the authority of Abu ʿAmir, and Hafs on the authority of ʿAsim recite the *ya* with a *fatha* in the words *(wa liya)*. Qunbul on the authority of Ibn Kathir, Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim, Hamza, al-Kisai, Abu Jaʿfar, Yaʿqub and Khalaf recite it with the *ya* sukun.

Surah al-Nasr

This surah was called, in the speech of the early generation (*al-salaf*), "the surah of *Idha ja'a nasrullahi wal-fath*" (When the help of Allah and the victory come). Al-Bukhari narrated that ʿAʾisha said: "When the surah *Idha ja'a nasrullahi wal-fath* was revealed..." and the hadith follows.

It is called in the Mushafs and in most of the tafsirs "the surah of al-Nasr" because the help of Allah is mentioned in it. It was thus named after *al-nasr*, which is known by a mention of the remembered kind.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi it is titled "the surah of al-Fath" because this word occurs in it. This name is therefore shared between it and *"Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory"* [al-Fath: 1].

From Ibn Masʿud it is reported that it is called "the surah of farewell" in al-Itqan (of al-Suyuti), because of the allusion in it to the farewell of the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: the indication of the approaching of his joining the Highest Companion, as will be cited from ʿAʾisha.

It is Medinan by consensus.

Scholars differed about the time of its revelation. It is said it was revealed upon the Prophet's (ﷺ) return from Khaybar, that is, in the year seven. This is supported by what al-Tabari and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Medina, *Idha ja'a nasrullahi wal-fath* was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allahu Akbar! The help of Allah and the victory have come, and the help of the people of Yemen has come.' A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who are the people of Yemen?' He said: 'A people whose hearts are tender and whose natures are gentle. Faith is Yemeni, understanding is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.'" The first arrival of the people of Yemen was the arrival of the delegation of the Ashʿaris in the year of the expedition of Khaybar.

The commentators have not differed that the intended victory in the verse is the conquest of Mecca. According to this, the victory is future, and the entry of people into religion in multitudes is also future, which is the most fitting use of *idha*. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), *"The help of Allah and the victory have come"* [al-Nasr: 1], is understood as the use of the past tense in the sense of the present, to express the certainty of its occurrence, or because the help at Khaybar was a prelude to the conquest of Mecca.

[p. 588]
It is narrated from Qatada: it was revealed two years before the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-Wahidi said on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: "It was revealed upon his return from Hunayn." Then the victory had already passed, and the entry of people into religion in multitudes is future. This was in the year of the delegations, the ninth year. According to this, *idha* is used merely to indicate time, without specifying it.

Al-Bazzar, al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Abi Shayba and ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that it was revealed in the middle of the days of *tashriq* (that is, in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage). Ibn Rajab weakened this, since it contains Musa ibn ʿUbayda, who is weak. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "Narration from him is not permissible, even if this narration is authentic." If this narration were sound, then the victory and the entry of people into religion in multitudes would already have passed.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived after its revelation about three months. According to this, *idha* is used for past time, since the victory and the entry of people into religion had already occurred.

Reports have converged, both in transmission and in interpretation, that this surah contains an allusion to the approaching of the appointed term of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). There is nothing in this that favours one of the opinions on the time of its revelation, for there is no disagreement that this allusion indicates the time of the coming of the help and the victory and the entry of people into religion in multitudes; when that occurs, the noble term has arrived.

In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas in Sahih al-Bukhari: "It is the term of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); he was informed of it. He said: *'Idha ja'a nasrullahi wal-fath'* [al-Nasr: 1], and that is the sign of your term. *'So glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness'* [al-Nasr: 3]."

In this is what explains some reports that mention an allusion to the approach of that term, such as the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas in al-Bayhaqi's Dala'il al-Nubuwwa and al-Darimi and Ibn Mardawayh: "When *Idha ja'a nasrullahi wal-fath* [al-Nasr: 1] was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Fatima and said: 'My soul has been announced to me,' and she wept." The statement "when it was revealed" is an insertion (*mudraj*) by the narrator; it is rather an announcement to her during his illness, as came in the hadith of his death in the two Sahihs. Thus this is a reconciliation of what appears to be a contradiction in this matter.

[p. 589]
Jabir ibn Zayd counted it as the one hundred and third surah in the order of revelation of the surahs, and said: "It was revealed after Surah al-Hashr and before Surah al-Nur." This accords with the narration that it was revealed immediately after the expedition of Khaybar.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was the last surah revealed of the Qur'an. Then, on his count, it would be the one hundred and fourteenth surah, revealed after Surah Bara'a, and no surah was revealed after it.

Its verses number three, and it is equal to Surah al-Kawthar in the number of verses, though it is longer than Surah al-Kawthar by several words, and shorter than Surah al-ʿAsr. These three are equal in the number of verses.

In the hadith of Ibn Abi Shayba, from Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi, in the narration of the stabbing of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf prayed a light prayer with the two shortest surahs of the Qur'an: *"Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar"* [al-Kawthar: 1] and *"When the help of Allah and the victory come"* [al-Nasr: 1].

* * *

The purpose of the surah is the promise of complete help from Allah, or of the conquest of Mecca, and the good news of the entry of a great multitude into Islam, through conquest or without it, if its revelation was at the Prophet's (ﷺ) return from Khaybar, as Ibn ʿAbbas said in one of his two opinions.

It also alludes to the fact that, when that occurs, the departure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the Hereafter has drawn near.

His promise that Allah has forgiven him with a complete forgiveness, such that there is no accountability for him thereafter for anything that might trouble his soul, the fear that some shortcoming might be on his part, which the limit of human strength necessitates, since human strength falls short of what his angelic aspiration seeks. Thus he has equalled the angelic limit which Allah, the Exalted, described for the angels in His saying: *"They glorify Him night and day; they never tire"* [al-Anbiya': 20].
